paragraphs.source_en: Sijistani reveled in reason and the life of learning and was consumed by the open questions that constantly arose during his evening discussions. At the same time he showed fulsome respect for religion and the revelations on which it is based, going so far as to declare that prophets rank higher than philosophers and scientists. 12 One suspects that this utterance included a big element of diplomacy.

ja.t: まれていたのではないかと

paragraphs.source_en: For having made this declaration, Sijistani went on to argue that religion and philosophy belong to totally separate realms and are in fact mutually incompatible. Religion, which he equated with religious law (Sharia), has neither need nor use for reason and inconvenient “Why?” questions. Its purpose, after all, is to affirm humanity’s subordination to God and to promote fear before Him, not to engage in argumentation. Conversely, the world of learning (“philosophy”) has no need or place for religion. In his Storehouse of Wisdom, Sijistani offered the striking conclusion that philosophers and scientists should completely separate themselves from religion, just as adepts of religion should distance themselves from all rational thought. It is clear that Sijistani had a tougher side.

paragraphs.source_en: At one of his sessions a young scholar from Bukhara had the temerity to complain about the financial aid he was receiving, pontificating that someone focused on learning should not have to bother about his sustenance. Sijistani archly replied that the Bukharan should consume less, and concentrate instead on achieving wisdom and virtue. That this young Bukharan dropped from history at this point suggests that his grant was not renewed. 13 162 • Chapter 6 Arab Colleagues To acknowledge the role of Central Asians in the “Arab Renaissance” is not to diminish the achievement of Arab scientists at Baghdad. They were there from the outset and played a noteworthy role.
